abstract.t:
Without a subscription, a cache can serve a stored response only while the response is fresh, and then has to ask the origin server whether the resource has changed. So a cache serves a resource that changes often either stale, or with a request to the origin server each time. This document defines how a cache subscribes to the resource, as any HTTP client can. The cache stores each response in the subscription as the response to a GET. While the subscription is continuously validating, the cache knows at every moment that its copy is current, so it can respond to requests with the copy, without asking the origin server, even for responses marked no-cache. When validation stops, the copy ages, and HTTP's rules for stale responses apply.
A cache can also serve many subscribers of its own from one subscription to the origin server, and keep private responses private. This document updates RFC 9111, so that a continuously validating subscription satisfies the no-cache directive.
This document is one of the Braid-HTTP extensions, which work alone or together; together they make HTTP a state synchronization protocol.
